key_terms.meaning: A = log₁₀(I₀/I), where I₀ is incident light intensity and I is transmitted intensity; it is dimensionless.
A = εcl, where ε is molar absorptivity, c is concentration, and l is light path length.
ε, a constant for a solute at a fixed wavelength; units are L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
Light emitted by thermally excited atoms in a flame; intensity at a fixed wavelength measures the element present.
A fixed amount of lithium in the diluent; the instrument reads Na/Li and K/Li ratios, which cancel flame and spray-rate changes.
A glass membrane whose potential changes with H⁺ activity, about 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C.
A CO₂ electrode: CO₂ diffuses through a membrane into bicarbonate solution, changing pH; this pH change gives pCO₂.
An oxygen electrode: O₂ diffuses through a membrane and is reduced at a cathode; current is proportional to pO₂.
A cell passing through an aperture displaces conducting electrolyte and raises resistance; each pulse is one cell.
Small opening through which diluted blood is drawn; pulse height depends on cell volume.
Instrument that pipettes sample and reagent, incubates, reads absorbance, and computes concentration.
A photometer with a fixed flow cell; absorbance is read as liquid passes, reducing manual cuvette handling.
Time from injection to detection of a solute in chromatography; used for identification under fixed conditions.
μ = v/E, where v is migration velocity and E is electric field strength; units are m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², with r in cm; it is centrifugal force as a multiple of g.
Movement of particles denser than the liquid outward in a spinning tube (lighter ones move inward); the speed depends on size, density difference and viscosity, v = d²Δρω²r/(18η).
Gas-filled detector that gives one large voltage pulse per ionising event, without energy information.
Scintillator converts radiation to light flashes; a photomultiplier converts them to pulses whose height follows energy.
Expected pCO₂ in a metabolic acidosis = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 mmHg; a measured pCO₂ outside this band means a second, respiratory disorder.
R<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by a spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front, on a TLC plate or paper; between 0 and 1.
The time τ after each GM pulse when the tube cannot count; true rate n = m/(1 − mτ) from the observed rate m.

takeaways: The Beer–Lambert law A = εcl makes absorbance, not transmittance, proportional to concentration; a blank sets A = 0 and a standard read at the same wavelength and path gives the unknown by ratio.

A flame photometer measures light emitted by sodium, potassium and lithium atoms in a flame; serum is diluted 1:50 to 1:200 in a lithium diluent, and the Na/Li and K/Li ratios cancel flame and spray changes.
A blood gas analyser holds a glass pH electrode, a Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode and a Clark pO₂ electrode at 37 °C; pH and pCO₂ set the acid–base state, pO₂ reports oxygenation.
Bicarbonate and base excess are calculated from pH and pCO₂ with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation; Winter's formula checks whether the breathing has compensated a metabolic acidosis.

A Coulter counter counts resistance pulses as cells pass a 100 µm aperture and sizes them by pulse height; red cells and platelets are counted at about 1:50 000, white cells on a separate lysed dilution near 1:500.

An automated analyser repeats photometry hundreds of times an hour: end-point tests are read by ratio to a calibrator, enzyme tests as ΔA/min, and carryover and bichromatic correction are checked on purpose.
Chromatography separates by partition between a mobile and a stationary phase (retention time on columns, R<sub>f</sub> on plates); electrophoresis separates charged molecules by mobility μ = v/E.
Centrifugal force grows with radius and with the square of speed, RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², so protocols are set in × g, not rpm.
A Geiger–Müller tube gives one equal pulse per event and loses counts in its dead time; a scintillation counter gives pulses whose height follows energy, so it can identify an isotope.
bank_note: Long answers usually expect a labelled block diagram, the operating sequence, the governing equation with one worked number, and an error source, for the spectrophotometer, flame photometer, blood gas electrodes, Coulter counter and automated analyser. Numerical questions use Beer–Lambert ratios, dilution factors, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and the RCF formula.

bank.q: State the Beer–Lambert law, define every term, and explain why absorbance is used instead of transmitted intensity for concentration measurement.
outline: Write A = εcl and define A, ε, c, l.
Explain A = log₁₀(I₀/I) and the linear relation to concentration.
State assumptions: monochromatic light, dilute solution, no scattering.
Give one clinical example such as glucose or haemoglobin measurement.
answer: Statement. When monochromatic light passes through a dilute solution, the absorbance is proportional to the concentration of the absorbing substance and to the length of the light path: A = εcl.

head: Symbol
Meaning
Unit
rows: light intensity leaving the blank, entering the sample
molar absorptivity of the substance at the chosen wavelength

answer: Where it comes from. Each thin slice of solution removes the same fraction of the light that reaches it, and that fraction is proportional to the number of molecules in the slice. Losing a fixed fraction per slice makes the intensity fall exponentially with path and with concentration: I = I₀ × 10−εcl. Taking the logarithm turns this into the straight line A = εcl.

Transmittance. T = I/I₀ is the fraction of light that gets through, so T = 10−A. T is not linear in concentration: doubling c doubles A but squares T. For A = 0.30, T = 0.50; for A = 0.60, T = 0.25, not 0.00.

Why absorbance is used. (1) A plot of A against c is a straight line through the origin with slope εl, so one standard and a blank are enough for a ratio calculation. (2) Equal steps in concentration give equal steps in A at any level, so errors are easy to read. (3) A is independent of the lamp brightness, because it is a ratio I₀/I taken against the blank; the raw intensity I changes when the lamp ages.

Worked number. A 0.20 mmol/L standard reads A = 0.30 in a 1.00 cm cuvette, so ε = 0.30 / (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L × 1.00 cm) = 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. A sample reading A = 0.45 is c = 0.45 / (1500 × 1.00) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L = 0.30 mmol/L. The ratio method gives the same: 0.20 × 0.45/0.30 = 0.30 mmol/L.

Conditions for the law. Monochromatic light, because ε changes with wavelength; a dilute, clear solution, because at high concentration molecules interact and above about A = 1.5 stray light bends the line; no scattering or fluorescence; the same cuvette path and temperature for standard and sample.

Clinical use. Haemoglobin is measured as cyanmethaemoglobin at 540 nm; glucose is measured after an enzyme reaction makes a coloured product, read near 505 nm. A sample that reads above the linear range is diluted by a known factor and the result multiplied back.
Check. Units: ε × c × l = (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹)(mol L⁻¹)(cm) has no unit, as A must; and 10−0.30 = 0.50 confirms the standard lets half the light through.

bank.q: Draw and explain the construction and working of a flame photometer for estimating sodium and potassium in serum.
outline: Label nebulizer, burner, flame, monochromator or filter, detector, and readout.
Explain atomisation, excitation, and emission at fixed wavelengths.
Describe calibration with standards and use of lithium internal standard.
Mention interference from other alkali metals and flame instability.
answer: Principle. Atoms of sodium, potassium and lithium in a hot flame absorb heat, rise to an excited state and fall back within about 10 ns, emitting light at wavelengths fixed by their electron levels: 589 nm (Na), 766 nm (K) and 671 nm (Li). The brightness of each line is proportional to the number of atoms of that element in the flame, and so to its concentration in the sprayed solution.

answer.pre:
diluted serum ─> nebulizer ─> burner + flame ─> lens ─> filter 589 / 766 / 671 nm ─> photodetector ─> amplifier ─> readout
                  ^      ^
                 air    LPG

answer: Sample preparation. Serum holds about 140 mmol/L sodium and 4 mmol/L potassium, far above the linear range, so it is diluted 1:50 to 1:200 in a diluent that already contains a fixed amount of lithium.

Nebulizer and burner. Compressed air draws the diluted sample up a fine capillary and breaks it into a spray; large drops fall to a drain and only the fine mist is carried with the fuel gas into the burner. Fuel is LPG (propane or butane) with air, giving about 1900 °C; air–acetylene gives about 2200–2300 °C. The cooler flame excites the alkali metals but few other elements.

Atomisation and excitation. In the flame the water evaporates, the salt particles melt and vaporise, and the molecules split into free atoms. A small, steady fraction of these atoms is excited at any instant, and their emission is the signal.

Optics and detection. A lens collects the light. Interference filters pass one line each to a photodetector. Each element has its own channel, so sodium, potassium and the lithium reference are read together. The 766 nm potassium line needs a red-sensitive detector such as a silicon photodiode.

Calibration. The diluent alone sets zero; a standard made at the diluted strength sets the scale. With a one-point calibration Cserum = Cstd × (Rsample/Rstd) × D. Example: 1:50 dilution, reading 40, standard 2.0 mmol/L reading 32: Cd = 2.0 × 40/32 = 2.5 mmol/L and Cserum = 2.5 × 50 = 125 mmol/L, which is low and is repeated before reporting.

Lithium internal standard. The instrument reads Na/Li and K/Li ratios. If the spray rate drops by 10 %, every line drops by 10 %, so the ratio is unchanged: a K/Li ratio of 0.42 against 0.50 for a 0.10 mmol/L standard still gives 0.10 × 0.84 × 50 = 4.2 mmol/L.

Interferences and errors. Other alkali metals leak through a broad filter; self-absorption by cooler atoms at the flame edge bends the curve down at high concentration; flame flicker and a partly blocked capillary give low, noisy readings; viscous or lipaemic samples spray less. The remedies are narrow filters, working on the linear part of the curve, the internal standard and regular cleaning.
Check. The three wavelengths are distinct (589, 671, 766 nm), so one lens can feed three filters without overlap; and 125 mmol/L is 2.5 × 50, consistent with the 1:50 dilution.

bank.q: Describe the three electrode systems of a blood gas analyser and state what each measures.
outline: Glass pH electrode: potential changes with H⁺ activity.
Severinghaus electrode: CO₂ changes internal bicarbonate pH, giving pCO₂.
Clark electrode: O₂ reduction at cathode gives current proportional to pO₂.
Explain common temperature control, membranes, electrolytes, and calibration.
answer: What is measured. pH and pCO₂, which together set the acid–base state, and pO₂, which reports oxygenation. The three electrodes sit in one chamber held at 37 °C, and the arterial sample flows past all three.

head: Electrode
Construction
Signal
Measures
rows: thin H⁺-sensitive glass bulb; Ag/AgCl reference in KCl
pH glass electrode behind a CO₂-permeable membrane, with a thin bicarbonate film between
platinum cathode at about −0.65 V against Ag/AgCl, under an O₂-permeable membrane

answer: pH electrode. H⁺ ions exchange at the hydrated glass surface and set up a potential E = E⁰ − (2.303RT/F) pH. At 310 K the slope is 2.303 × 8.314 × 310/96 485 = 0.0615 V, so 61.5 mV per pH unit; a fall from 7.40 to 7.20 raises the cell voltage by 12.3 mV. The glass has a very high resistance, so the amplifier needs a very high input impedance.

Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode. CO₂ diffuses through the membrane into the bicarbonate film and forms carbonic acid, CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The film pH falls by about one unit for each tenfold rise in pCO₂, and the glass electrode reads it. Calibration with two gases of known pCO₂ turns the voltage into mmHg. Response takes a minute or two because CO₂ must diffuse.

Clark pO₂ electrode. Oxygen crossing the membrane is reduced at the cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. At the polarising voltage every arriving O₂ molecule is reduced, so the current, in nanoamperes, is proportional to pO₂. Calibration uses a zero-oxygen solution and a gas of known pO₂.

Calculated values. Bicarbonate from Henderson–Hasselbalch, [HCO₃⁻] = 0.03 × pCO₂ × 10(pH − 6.1); for pH 7.32 and pCO₂ 30 mmHg this is 0.90 × 101.22 = 0.90 × 16.6 = 15 mmol/L. Base excess is the strong acid needed to bring the blood back to pH 7.40 at pCO₂ 40 mmHg.

Common features. (1) The 37 °C chamber, because all three electrode outputs and the blood equilibria change with temperature; for a cooled patient the analyser corrects to the patient temperature. (2) Membranes that must be intact and clean. (3) Electrolyte fillings renewed on schedule. (4) Two-point calibration with buffers and gases, and quality control material each shift.
Errors. An air bubble raises pO₂ and lowers pCO₂; a delay lowers pO₂ and raises pCO₂ through white cell metabolism; a protein film on the membrane slows the response.
Check. log₁₀(15/0.90) = log₁₀ 16.7 = 1.22 and 6.1 + 1.22 = 7.32, so the calculated bicarbonate is consistent with the measured pH and pCO₂.

bank.q: Explain the Coulter principle and how a blood cell counter obtains both cell count and cell size.
outline: Describe aperture, electrolyte, electrodes, and current path.
Cell displaces electrolyte and raises resistance; one pulse per cell.
Pulse count gives cell number; pulse height gives volume.
Mention dilution, threshold setting, and coincidence error.
answer: Principle. A blood cell is a poor conductor compared with the saline around it. When it passes through a small aperture it pushes conducting liquid out of the way, so the resistance of the aperture rises for the few microseconds the cell is inside. With a constant current I, the rise ΔR gives a voltage pulse ΔV = I × ΔR.

Construction. A glass tube with a sapphire aperture about 100 µm across stands in a beaker of diluted blood. One electrode is inside the tube and one outside, joined to a constant-current source. A vacuum or a metering pump draws an exact volume, for example 0.50 mL, through the aperture. The pulses go to an amplifier, threshold discriminators, a scaler and a pulse-height analyser.

Count. Each pulse above the threshold is one cell. Cells per litre = (N/V) × D × 1000 with V in mL. Example: 48 000 red cell pulses in 0.50 mL at 1:50 000 give 96 000 per mL × 50 000 × 1000 = 4.8 × 1012 per litre.

Size. The resistance change, and so the pulse height, is proportional to the volume of electrolyte displaced, that is to cell volume. A pulse-height analyser sorts the pulses into channels and draws a volume histogram; the mean of the red cell histogram is the mean cell volume (MCV), about 80–100 fL.
Why two dilutions. Whole blood has about 1000 red cells per white cell, so white cells are counted on a separate portion after a lysing reagent destroys the red cells.

Coincidence error. If two cells are in the aperture together they give one large pulse: the count is low and the size is wrong. High dilution keeps the chance small, and instruments add a correction of a few percent. Accidental under-dilution, say 1:5000 instead of 1:50 000, makes the loss large.

Other errors. A partly blocked aperture changes pulse heights and adds noise pulses; thresholds set too low count debris as platelets; giant platelets or clumps can be counted as red or white cells. Instruments monitor the aperture current and the time to draw the metered volume.
Check. 4.8 × 1012 per litre is 4.8 million per µL, inside the adult range of 4.5–5.5 × 1012 per litre, so the dilution factor has been applied the right way round.

bank.q: Compare chromatography and electrophoresis as separation methods, naming the property each uses.
outline: Chromatography uses partition between mobile and stationary phases.
Electrophoresis uses charge and size in an electric field.
Compare mobile phase, support medium, detection, and typical clinical uses.
Give examples such as HbA1c by chromatography and serum protein electrophoresis.
answer: Common aim. Both methods separate the parts of a mixture so each can be measured; both give a record of signal against time or position, read by a detector or a densitometer.

Chromatography: the property used. Partition (or adsorption) between a moving mobile phase and a fixed stationary phase. A solute moves only while it is in the mobile phase, so a solute held longer by the stationary phase travels more slowly. Columns report retention time tR; plates and paper report Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent-front distance, for example 2.0/8.0 = 0.25.

Electrophoresis: the property used. Charge and friction in an electric field. A molecule of charge q in field E feels force qE and drifts at v = μE = qE/f. The sign of the charge depends on buffer pH relative to the isoelectric point; size and shape set the friction.

head: Feature
Chromatography
Electrophoresis
rows: column packing, plate coating or paper
paper, cellulose acetate, agarose, polyacrylamide, capillary
FID in GC; UV in HPLC
stain and densitometer; UV in capillary

answer: Clinical examples. HbA1c by ion-exchange HPLC, read near 415 nm; drug levels and urine steroids by GC or HPLC. Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6 gives albumin, α₁, α₂, β and γ; haemoglobin variants by electrophoresis or capillary methods; DNA in agarose gels.

Worked number. Total protein 70 g/L with albumin 60 % gives albumin 0.60 × 70 = 42 g/L and γ 15 % gives 0.15 × 70 = 10.5 g/L. On a 10 cm strip at 200 V (E = 2000 V/m), albumin moving 3.0 cm in 40 min has v = 0.030/2400 = 1.25 × 10−5 m/s and μ = 6.25 × 10−9 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Choosing. Use chromatography for small neutral or weakly charged molecules (drugs, steroids, amino acids, HbA1c); use electrophoresis for proteins and nucleic acids, where charge and size are the natural handles.
Check. The five protein fractions add to 60 + 4 + 9 + 12 + 15 = 100 %, so the g/L values add back to 70 g/L.

bank.q: A solution of concentration 0.20 mmol L⁻¹ gives absorbance 0.40 in a 1.0 cm cuvette. Calculate ε and the concentration when absorbance is 0.30 under the same conditions.
outline: Show unit cancellation and state proportionality.
Note that the same wavelength and cuvette are assumed.
answer: Given. c = 0.20 mmol/L, A = 0.40, l = 1.0 cm; a second reading A = 0.30 under the same wavelength and cuvette.
Find ε. From A = εcl: ε = A/(cl) = 0.40 / (0.20 mmol/L × 1.0 cm) = 2.0 L mmol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
Same value in molar units. 0.20 mmol/L = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L, so ε = 0.40 / (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.0) = 2000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Both lines give the same ε, in different units.
Find the new concentration. c = A/(εl) = 0.30 / (2.0 L mmol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ × 1.0 cm) = 0.15 mmol/L.
Ratio method. Because A is proportional to c, c = 0.20 × (0.30/0.40) = 0.15 mmol/L, the same answer without finding ε.

Transmittances. For A = 0.40, T = 10−0.40 = 0.398; for A = 0.30, T = 10−0.30 = 0.501. T rose by about 26 % while c fell by 25 %; T follows a curve, not a straight line, so it is not used for the calculation.

Assumptions. The same wavelength (ε depends on it), the same 1.0 cm cuvette, a blank subtracted from both readings, and both absorbances inside the linear range (well below about 1.5). The solution must be clear, with no scattering.

Linear range. Both readings, 0.40 and 0.30, lie well below about A = 1.5, where stray light starts to bend the calibration line, and well above about 0.05, where noise dominates; so a straight-line ratio is valid. A reading of 2.0 would mean c = 1.0 mmol/L on paper, but the true value could be higher; the sample would be diluted, say 1:5, read again and the result multiplied by 5.

Effect of path length. If the second reading had been taken in a 0.5 cm cuvette, A = εcl would halve for the same concentration. Reading A = 0.30 in that cell means c = 0.30/(2.0 × 0.5) = 0.30 mmol/L, twice the 1 cm answer. Standard and sample must share the same path.
Check. εcl = 2.0 × 0.15 × 1.0 = 0.30, the given absorbance.

bank.q: A 1:50 diluted serum sample gives 47 units on a flame photometer; a 3.0 mmol L⁻¹ sodium standard gives 50 units. Find serum sodium concentration and discuss one interference.
outline: Multiply by the dilution factor: 2.82 × 50 = 141 mmol L⁻¹, within 135–145.
Spray-rate change, flame drift and self-absorption at high concentration can bias emission.
A lithium internal standard cancels spray and flame changes.
answer: Given. Dilution 1:50, so D = 50. Sample reading Rsample = 47; standard Cstd = 3.0 mmol/L (at diluted strength) reading Rstd = 50.
Diluted concentration. Emission is proportional to concentration on the linear part of the curve, so Cd = Cstd × Rsample/Rstd = 3.0 × 47/50 = 3.0 × 0.94 = 2.82 mmol/L.
Serum concentration. Cserum = Cd × D = 2.82 × 50 = 141 mmol/L.
Interpretation. The reference range is about 135–145 mmol/L, so 141 mmol/L is normal.

One interference: spray-rate and flame changes. If the sample is more viscous than the standard (high protein or lipid), less of it is sprayed and the reading falls. A 6 % drop would turn 47 units into 44.2, and the result into 3.0 × 44.2/50 × 50 = 132.6 mmol/L, a false hyponatraemia. Flame flicker and a partly blocked capillary act the same way.

Remedy. A lithium internal standard in the diluent: the Na/Li ratio does not change when both lines fall by the same 6 %, so the result stays 141 mmol/L. Matching the standard to the sample matrix and cleaning the capillary also help.

Other interferences. Self-absorption at high concentration bends the curve down, so calibration should bracket the sample; light from potassium or calcium can leak through a broad sodium filter; ionisation in a hot flame lowers the atom population.

Bracketing the sample. With two standards of 2.0 and 3.0 mmol/L reading 34 and 50 units, the line between them has slope (50 − 34)/1.0 = 16 units per mmol/L; 47 units then gives 2.0 + (47 − 34)/16 = 2.81 mmol/L, the same as the one-point answer within 0.01, which shows the curve is straight in this range.
Other units. Sodium has a molar mass of 23 g/mol, so 141 mmol/L = 141 × 23 = 3243 mg/L, about 324 mg/dL; some older reports use mEq/L, which for a singly charged ion is the same number as mmol/L.
Check. 141/50 = 2.82 mmol/L and 2.82/3.0 = 0.94 = 47/50, so the numbers are consistent.

bank.q: For a blood sample at 37 °C, pH = 7.30 and pCO₂ = 45 mmHg. Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation, calculate bicarbonate in mmol L⁻¹.
outline: Rearrange: [HCO₃⁻] = 0.03 × pCO₂ × 10<sup>(pH − 6.1)</sup>.
pH 7.30 is acidaemia; HCO₃⁻ slightly low; pCO₂ 45 is above the 38–42 mmHg that Winter's formula predicts.
So a mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis; base excess is a calculated index.
answer: Given. pH = 7.30, pCO₂ = 45 mmHg, at 37 °C. Henderson–Hasselbalch for blood: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × pCO₂)).
Rearrange. log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × pCO₂)) = pH − 6.1, so [HCO₃⁻] = 0.03 × pCO₂ × 10(pH − 6.1).
Classify. pH 7.30 is below 7.35: acidaemia. HCO₃⁻ 21.4 mmol/L is just below 22: a metabolic acidosis is present. pCO₂ 45 mmHg is at the top of 35–45: the lungs are not blowing off CO₂.
Check compensation with Winter's formula. Expected pCO₂ = 1.5 × 21.4 + 8 = 40.1 ± 2, that is 38.1–42.1 mmHg. The measured 45 mmHg is higher, so CO₂ is being retained as well.
Conclusion. A mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis, for example a patient with mild ketoacidosis whose breathing is depressed. In a simple metabolic acidosis the pCO₂ would be near 40 or lower.
Base excess. Base excess is calculated from pH, pCO₂ and haemoglobin and shows the metabolic part alone; here it would be slightly negative (a small base deficit), confirming the metabolic component.
Sources of error. A kPa value put into the mmHg formula (45 mmHg is 6.0 kPa), an air bubble lowering pCO₂, or a delayed sample raising it.

Where the numbers come from. The glass electrode gives the pH and the Severinghaus electrode the pCO₂; the analyser computes bicarbonate from them, exactly as above, so an error in pCO₂ carries straight into HCO₃⁻.

Total CO₂ and units. Total CO₂ = HCO₃⁻ + 0.03 × pCO₂ = 21.4 + 1.35 = 22.8 mmol/L. In kPa, 45 mmHg × 0.1333 = 6.0 kPa; a formula written for mmHg needs the mmHg value, or the 0.03 factor must change to 0.23 mmol/(L·kPa).

Contrast. Had the pCO₂ been 40 mmHg with the same HCO₃⁻, pH = 6.1 + log₁₀(21.4/1.20) = 6.1 + 1.25 = 7.35, at the lower limit of normal; the extra 5 mmHg of retained CO₂ is what pulls the pH down to 7.30.

bank.q: A white cell dilution of 1:250 is drawn through a Coulter aperture; 0.200 mL gives 6400 pulses. Calculate white cells per µL and per litre of whole blood and state one coincidence limitation.
outline: Diluted count = 6400 / 0.200 mL = 32 000 per mL.
Multiply by 250: 8.0 × 10⁶ per mL of blood = 8000 per µL.
Per litre: 8.0 × 10⁹, inside 4–11 × 10⁹.
Coincidence: two cells in the aperture at once count as one pulse; it grows with concentration.
answer: Given. Dilution 1:250, so D = 250; volume drawn V = 0.200 mL; pulses N = 6400, red cells lysed.
Count in the dilution. N/V = 6400 / 0.200 mL = 32 000 cells per mL of dilution.
Count in whole blood. 32 000 × 250 = 8.0 × 10⁶ cells per mL of blood.
Per µL and per litre. 1 mL = 1000 µL, so 8.0 × 10⁶ / 1000 = 8000 per µL. 1 L = 1000 mL, so 8.0 × 10⁶ × 1000 = 8.0 × 109 per litre.
Interpretation. The white cell reference range is 4–11 × 109 per litre, so 8.0 × 109 is normal.

Coincidence limitation. Two cells inside the aperture at the same moment give one pulse, so the count is low. The chance rises with concentration. As an estimate, if the sensing zone of a 100 µm aperture holds about 6 × 10⁻⁷ mL, the mean number of cells in it is 32 000 × 6 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 0.02, so about 2 % of cells arrive while another is present. Counters correct for this by a formula or keep the dilution high.
Why the red cells must be lysed. Without lysis this 1:250 dilution would hold about 2 × 10⁷ red cells per mL, more than 600 for every white cell, and coincidence would be severe.

Manual cross-check. On a Neubauer chamber at 1:20 the four large corner squares hold 0.4 µL. With 8000 cells per µL of blood the dilution holds 8000/20 = 400 per µL, so the technician should count about 400 × 0.4 = 160 cells. A count near 160 confirms the analyser.
How reports print it. Many reports give 8.0 × 10³ per µL; this is the same number as 8000 per µL and as 8.0 × 109 per litre.
Check. Working backwards, 8.0 × 10⁶ per mL ÷ 250 × 0.200 mL = 32 000 × 0.200 = 6400 pulses, the count given.

bank.q: An automated analyser takes 18 s per test channel and runs 20 channels in parallel. Calculate theoretical tests per hour and explain why carryover and reagent dead volume reduce this figure.
outline: Per channel: 3600/18 = 200 tests per hour.
Twenty channels: 200 × 20 = 4000 tests per hour theoretical.
Carryover needs wash steps between samples.
Reagent dead volume, calibration, and quality control reduce throughput.
answer: Given. 18 s per test on each channel, 20 channels working in parallel.
One channel. 3600 s per hour ÷ 18 s per test = 200 tests per hour.
Twenty channels. 200 × 20 = 4000 tests per hour in theory, that is one result every 3600/4000 = 0.9 s on average.
What the figure means. It is the rate at which results come out, not the time one test takes; each test still incubates for several minutes while the others run beside it.

Carryover and washing. A trace of the previous sample or reagent on the probe raises the next result. Carryover is measured with a high–low run: if H3 = 29.8, L1 = 5.30 and L3 = 5.10 mmol/L, carryover = (5.30 − 5.10)/(29.8 − 5.10) × 100 % = 0.81 %. Extra wash cycles reduce it, but each costs a cycle that produces no result.
Reagent dead volume. Every bottle has a volume the probe cannot reach, and on-board reagents age; bottles must be changed and the test recalibrated, stopping that channel for a while.
Other limits. Not every sample needs every test, so some channels idle; emergency samples interrupt the sequence; sample loading and barcode reading take time.
Conclusion. The analyser delivers roughly 3300 tests per hour, about 83 % of the theoretical 4000. These shares are illustrative; each laboratory measures its own.

In samples. With losses the average interval is 3600/3317 = 1.09 s per result. If each patient sample needs 8 tests, the analyser finishes about 3317/8 = 415 samples per hour, and a morning load of 500 samples takes about 500/415 = 1.2 hours.

Why channels matter. A single channel on the same 18 s cycle gives only 200 tests per hour; twenty channels multiply the output twenty-fold but also multiply the reagent bottles, calibrations and controls to manage.

bank.q: A centrifuge rotor has radius 10 cm and spins at 3000 rpm. Calculate RCF in ×g and explain why a 5 cm rotor at the same rpm gives a different force.
outline: Use RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)².
For r = 10 cm: RCF ≈ 1006 ×g.
For r = 5 cm: RCF ≈ 503 ×g.
RCF depends on radius as well as speed.
answer: Formula. RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², with r in cm from the spindle to the tube bottom, giving a multiple of g.
Where the constant comes from. RCF = ω²r/g with ω = 2π(rpm)/60 and r in m. For r in cm: (2π/60)² × 0.01 / 9.81 = 0.010966 × 0.01 / 9.81 = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵.
Check by angular speed. ω = 2π × 3000/60 = 314.2 rad/s; ω²r = 314.2² × 0.10 = 9870 m/s²; 9870/9.81 = 1006, the same.

Why the 5 cm rotor gives a different force. At the same rpm both tubes turn at the same angular speed, but the tube on the 5 cm rotor moves in a smaller circle at half the linear speed. The centripetal acceleration ω²r is proportional to r, so halving r halves the force: 503 × g instead of 1006 × g.

Consequence for protocols. A protocol that says "3000 rpm" means different things on different rotors. Protocols are written in × g. To give the small rotor 1006 × g, rpm = √(1006/(1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 5)) = √(1.80 × 10⁷) = 4242 rpm.
Effect on separation. Settling speed is proportional to RCF (Stokes' law, v = d²Δρω²r/(18η)), so at 503 × g a serum spin needs about twice as long to pack the cells as at 1006 × g.

Practical note. In a swing-out rotor r is measured to the tube bottom with the bucket swung out; in a fixed-angle rotor r differs between the top and the bottom of the tube, and the maximum radius is usually quoted.

Fixed-angle example. In a fixed-angle rotor where the tube runs from r = 4 cm at the top to r = 8 cm at the bottom, 3000 rpm gives 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 4 × 9.0 × 10⁶ = 402 × g at the top and 805 × g at the bottom; the quoted figure is the maximum, 805 × g.
Check. 1006/503 = 2.0, matching the ratio of radii 10/5.

bank.q: A bench spectrophotometer and an automated analyser use the same Beer–Lambert law but give different serum glucose values. Analyse possible causes and state checks.
outline: Check wavelength, path length, blank, and calibration.
Check reagent age, temperature, incubation time, and sample volume.
Consider carryover, flow-cell dirt, turbidity, and lipaemia.
Verify with controls, duplicate samples, and manual comparison.
answer: Starting point. Both read A = εcl and convert by ratio to a calibrator, so a difference must come from something that changes A, ε, l or the calibration in one instrument and not the other. Suppose the bench gives 7.33 mmol/L and the analyser 7.50 mmol/L on the same serum.

Optical causes. (1) Wavelength: a bench filter at 520 nm instead of 505 nm changes ε, but the ratio cancels this only if standard and sample are read at the same setting and inside the linear range. (2) Path length: a 1 cm bench cuvette and a 0.6 cm analyser cell give different A, cancelled only if each is calibrated on its own. (3) Stray light and a worn lamp bend the line at high A.

Blank handling. If the bench user forgets to subtract a reagent blank of 0.02: raw sample A 0.44 and raw calibrator A 0.30 give 5.0 × 0.44/0.30 = 7.33 mmol/L, while the analyser's net values 0.42 and 0.28 give 5.0 × 0.42/0.28 = 7.50 mmol/L. That 0.17 mmol/L gap is the whole difference in this example.

head: Factor
Bench
Analyser
Effect
rows: slower colour at 25 °C; incomplete if read early
end point not reached reads low
a 2 % pipetting error gives a 2 % result error

answer: Sample causes. Lipaemia and a dirty cuvette add absorbance; the analyser's bichromatic reading removes most of it, the single-wavelength bench reading does not. Haemolysis is not removed by either and is flagged by the haemolysis index. Carryover from a high previous sample raises an analyser result.

Checks. (1) Run the same control serum on both; the one outside its limits is at fault. (2) Recalibrate both with the same calibrator lot. (3) Read the bench blank and subtract it. (4) Confirm wavelength and path settings. (5) Repeat in duplicate and compare with a reference method or an external quality scheme.
Conclusion. Most bench–analyser differences come from blanking, timing and temperature rather than from the law itself.
Check. 7.50 − 7.33 = 0.17 mmol/L, a 2.3 % difference, larger than typical glucose imprecision, so it is worth chasing.

bank.q: For the same patient the laboratory reports serum sodium 112 mmol/L by flame photometry and a red cell count of 7.4 × 10¹² per litre by a Coulter counter, both on dilutions made by one automatic diluter. Evaluate whether a dilution error, a calibration error or coincidence can explain both results, and outline verification steps.
outline: A dilution error moves both results the same way; here they move in opposite directions.
Coincidence lowers a count, so it cannot explain a high count.
Look for separate causes: flame calibration, nebulizer, internal standard, lipaemia; counter threshold, clog, haemoconcentration.
Verify with controls, fresh dilutions and an independent method such as an ion-selective electrode.
answer: The two results. Sodium 112 mmol/L against a reference of 135–145 mmol/L: low. Red cells 7.4 × 1012 per litre against 4.5–5.5: high.

Can one dilution error explain both? Over-dilution lowers every concentration and count; under-dilution raises them. To read 140 mmol/L as 112, the sodium dilution must have been 140/112 = 1.25 times too great. To read 5.0 × 1012 as 7.4, the red cell dilution must have been 7.4/5.0 = 1.48 times too small. One diluter fault cannot over-dilute one sample and under-dilute the other, so a single dilution error does not explain both.
Can coincidence explain the count? No. Coincidence merges two cells into one pulse and lowers the count. It cannot raise it.
Can calibration explain both? The two instruments are calibrated separately, so a shared calibration error is unlikely. Each must be checked on its own.

head: Result
Instrument cause
Patient cause
rows: standard made up wrong; flame drift; partly blocked capillary; lithium internal standard missing
true hyponatraemia; very high lipids or protein, which take up serum volume (pseudohyponatraemia)
threshold set too low; noise pulses from a partial clog; diluter under-delivering diluent
polycythaemia; dehydration (but that would raise sodium, not lower it)

answer: Verification steps. (1) Run control material on both instruments. (2) Check the diluter volume gravimetrically: 1.000 g of water should be delivered as 1.000 mL. (3) Repeat both tests on fresh, hand-made dilutions. (4) Measure sodium by a direct ion-selective electrode, which is not affected by lipid volume. (5) Check the haematocrit and haemoglobin: a true red cell count of 7.4 × 1012 per litre with an MCV of 90 fL gives a haematocrit of 7.4 × 1012 × 90 × 10−15 = 0.67, which should be visible on a spun tube. (6) Look at the sample for lipaemia.
Judgement. The pattern points to two independent problems, or to one real disorder plus one analytical error, not to one shared cause. Neither result is reported until the checks agree.
Report. Until the checks agree, the laboratory holds both results, records the fault found, and tells the ward that a repeat sample may be needed.
Check. 1.25 and 1.48 are in opposite directions from 1.00, confirming that no single dilution factor fits both.

bank.q: Compare a Geiger–Müller counter and a scintillation detector for measuring a low-activity radioimmunoassay label; choose one and justify by efficiency, energy information, and quenching.
outline: GM tube gives one large pulse per event and little energy information.
Scintillation counter gives pulse height related to energy and higher efficiency for gamma.
Quenching and background affect low-activity counting.
Choose scintillation for low activity and energy discrimination; choose GM for simple surveys.
answer: The label. Iodine-125 decays by electron capture and emits low-energy photons of about 27–35 keV; a radioimmunoassay tube holds a small activity, so counting efficiency and background decide the precision.

GM counter. Each event gives one equal pulse of about 1 V, so there is no energy information and background from other radiation cannot be rejected. Low-energy photons mostly pass through the gas without ionising it, so the efficiency for ¹²⁵I is very low, of the order of 1 %. Dead time is 100–200 µs.

Scintillation counter. A NaI(Tl) crystal, usually a well type with the tube inside the crystal, absorbs most of the low-energy photons and gives a flash whose brightness follows the energy; a photomultiplier and pulse-height window count only the ¹²⁵I photopeak. Efficiency is high, of the order of 70–80 %, and background outside the window is rejected.

answer.text: Numbers for a 200 Bq tube counted for 60 s (illustrative efficiencies).

answer: Quenching. Quenching belongs to liquid scintillation counting, used for weak beta labels such as tritium and carbon-14: coloured or chemical impurities in the cocktail absorb light or energy and lower the efficiency, so it is corrected with an external standard or a quench curve. A NaI(Tl) well counter for ¹²⁵I counts photons that leave the tube, so the sample chemistry does not quench it; the GM tube has its own gas quench, which only ends each discharge.
Dead time. If a GM tube had to count 150 per s with a 200 µs dead time, mτ = 0.03 and it would lose 3 %; scintillation counters have dead times of a few microseconds and lose almost nothing.

Choice. The NaI(Tl) well scintillation counter: about 75 times more counts, a tenfold smaller relative error in the same time, energy discrimination against background, and no quench problem for ¹²⁵I. The GM counter is kept for contamination surveys and simple bench checks, where cost and ruggedness matter more than precision.
Check. 9000/120 = 75, the ratio of the efficiencies, and the relative errors scale roughly as 1/√counts.
